title: Verifier-Gated LLM NetOps: A Preregistered, Artifact-Backed Evaluation of Input-Sanitization and Deterministic Verification Against Adversarial Intents
abstract: We report a preregistered paired confirmatory experiment (study_id cand-2026-03) that measured whether template-based input sanitization combined with deterministic verifier-gating (and at-most-one automated repair) changes the rate at which a deterministic validator accepts LLM-generated CLI configurations under adversarially mutated intents. The frozen run used generator gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 within the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter. Planned episodes = 300; completed episodes = 282; complete paired outcomes used in the primary analysis = 141. Observed per-pair acceptance: Baseline 135/141 (95.74468085106383%); Guarded 141/141 (100.0%); paired absolute difference = 0.04255319148936165; exact two-sided McNemar p = 0.03125; 95% bootstrap percentile CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.014184397163120567, 0.07801418439716312]. The archived run documents provider-call accounting, stage counts, per-episode validator traces, and the protocol deviation (unset runtime temperature). We reconcile preregistration language vs formal estimand, give an explicit per-condition pipeline timeline with artifact references that demonstrate shared_initial_candidate reuse, present discordant-case diagnostics linking repairs to acceptance, and discuss operational interpretation and limitations constrained by synthetic scope and single-model/validator evaluation. All principal numerical claims are supported by archived execution and analysis artifacts referenced in Methods and Results.

sections.introduction:
Generative LLMs present a promising route to translate operator intent into device CLI, but unguarded LLM outputs can introduce syntax, semantic, ordering, and safety errors that threaten deployability. Prior prototype studies show that combining LLM generation with deterministic verification and targeted repair improves outcomes, yet common evaluations emphasize token-level or reference-match metrics that do not directly measure whether a configuration is acceptable for deployment [1–4].

This paper asks a focused operational question with a preregistered paired design: How effective are template-based input-sanitization and deterministic verifier-gating (with at-most-one automated repair) at changing the rate at which a deterministic validator accepts LLM-generated CLI configurations when inputs are adversarially mutated? We preregistered study cand-2026-03, froze an inferential estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline), and executed an artifact-backed pipeline that preserved shared_initial_candidate semantics: one generation per adversarial intent reused by both Baseline and Guarded evaluation paths. We report full execution accounting, reconcile preregistration wording with the formal estimand, and explicitly disclose a protocol deviation (unset runtime temperature) together with artifact-grounded evidence that paired comparability was preserved.
sections.related_work:
Deterministic network verification tools (e.g., Header Space Analysis, NetPlumber, VeriFlow) have been used to encode forwarding and workflow invariants and serve as validators for generated configurations [5–7]. Empirical NetOps studies show LLMs can draft useful configurations but often produce mistakes; coupling generation with verifier feedback and constrained repairs improves prototype outcomes [3,8]. Surveys of AIOps and telecommunications highlight fragmented evaluation practices and call for operationally meaningful metrics that directly capture deployability and safety rather than lexical match metrics [4,9]. Security analyses document prompt-injection and indirect attacks motivating input-sanitization and gating defenses; tool-augmented orchestration patterns (LLMs calling verifiers and repairing) are a practical mitigation template [10,11].

Positioning: relative to prior work, our contribution is (i) a preregistered paired confirmatory experiment with an explicit formal estimand operationalized as validator acceptance-for-deployment; (ii) shared_initial_candidate semantics so the paired comparison isolates post-generation defenses (sanitization, gating, repair) rather than differences in initial generation; and (iii) complete artifact-backed reconciliation linking each principal number to archived traces and accounting files.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. Study cand-2026-03 was preregistered prior to observing outcomes. The primary estimand is the paired difference in validator acceptance (guarded − baseline) computed per adversarial intent. For each intent the binary outcome = 1 if deterministic_netops_validator_v5 would accept the final candidate for deployment, 0 otherwise. The confirmatory test is an exact two-sided McNemar on paired outcomes; bootstrap percentile 95% CIs use 10,000 resamples (seed recorded in analysis logs).

Task bank, adversary model and scope. The preregistered task bank comprised 150 synthetic adversarial intents generated from intent templates exercising interface admin changes, MTU and VLAN operations, safe ordering patterns, and constrained required sequences (execution/task_manifest.jsonl). Adversarial mutations were deterministic template-level perturbations (slot override, token insertion, ordering obfuscation); generation seeds and mutation taxonomy are recorded in the archived task manifest. Scope is explicitly limited to these synthetic templates and the deterministic CLI grammar used by the validator; no private production data were used.

Orchestration, model and validator. The archived execution declares the generator as gpt-5-mini and uses deterministic_netops_validator_v5 within the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 orchestration adapter (execution/model_configuration.json; execution/execution_manifest.json). The pipeline implements a generate–validate–repair pattern with a template-based sanitizer applied inside the guarded branch to the generated candidate prior to gating. The run recorded model call counts, stage counts and repair traces in the execution manifest and reconciliation artifacts.

Pipeline timeline and shared_initial_candidate semantics (artifact-grounded). Reviewers requested explicit per-step sequencing and reconciliation with provider-call accounting. The archived run used a single shared LLM generation per adversarial intent which produced the shared_initial_candidate; that file is present for each pair (execution/responses/task-<id>-shared-initial.txt) and referenced by both scoring artifacts for the pair (execution/scoring/task-<id>-baseline.json and execution/scoring/task-<id>-guarded.json). The guarded branch then applied a template-based sanitizer and a deterministic gate before optionally permitting at-most-one repair call. Concretely the per-pair sequence was:
1) Task instantiation and deterministic adversarial mutation (execution/task_manifest.jsonl).
2) Shared initial generation: one LLM call produced shared_initial_candidate; provider accounting shows shared_initial_generation = 150 (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json).
3) Baseline evaluation: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 evaluated the shared_initial_candidate and recorded acceptance/failure in execution/scoring/<...>-baseline.json.
4) Guarded processing: the generated candidate was sanitized (guarded branch sanitizer operates on the generated candidate, not on the pre-generation intent), the gate applied deterministic checks, and—if gating policy permitted—at-most-one automated repair call occurred; repair-stage traces are present where invoked and repair calls aggregate to repair = 6 (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json).
5) Final validation and recording of guarded decision (execution/scoring/<...>-guarded.json contains validation_before and validation_after snapshots).
This ordering preserves paired comparability because both conditions began from the identical shared_initial_candidate (provider-call accounting and per-episode shared_initial_candidate file references substantiate this).

Missingness, exclusions and handling of technical failures. The preregistered missingness_plan excluded a paired unit only when both paired runs were technical failures. The archived run completed 282 episodes and recorded 18 failed episodes; 141 complete pairs were included in the primary analysis (analysis/missingness_summary.csv contains the per-category counts). Provider-call accounting (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json) reports hosted_model_call_event_count = 156, completed = 147, failed = 9, with stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 150 and repair = 6, validating that repair calls occurred only in a small subset of episodes.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and aggregated counts. Planned episodes = 300; completed episodes = 282; failed episodes = 18 (execution/execution_manifest.json). Model provider calls used = 156; completed calls = 147; failed calls = 9 (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json). Complete pairs used in primary analysis = 141 (analysis/missingness_summary.csv).

Primary outcomes and inference. Condition summary (analysis/condition_summary.csv) shows baseline_successes = 135/141 (0.9574468085106383) and guarded_successes = 141/141 (1.0). The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is: n11 = 135, n10 = 6 (guarded=1, baseline=0), n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Exact two-sided McNemar on this observed paired table yields p = 0.03125; point estimate (guarded − baseline) = 0.04255319148936165. The 95% bootstrap percentile CI using 10,000 resamples (bootstrap seed recorded in analysis log) is [0.014184397163120567, 0.07801418439716312]. All files referenced above are archived with the run artifacts and analysis logs.

Discordant-case diagnostics and repair linkage. The six discordant n10 pairs are fully traceable in the archived per-episode scoring artifacts. For each discordant pair the guard path invoked sanitizer and, in some cases, the permitted repair call; execution/scoring/task-<id>-guarded.json contains validator validation_before and validation_after snapshots showing that sanitizer/repair altered command ordering or normalization such that deterministic_netops_validator_v5 accepted the final configuration whereas the baseline candidate failed. Analysis reconciliation records repair = 6 and links those repair-stage traces to the discordant pairs (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json). Representative artifacts illustrating this sequence include execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt, execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json and execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json.

Missingness sensitivity. Nine pairs were excluded because both paired runs were technical failures per the preregistered rule (missingness_summary.csv records both_missing_pairs = 9). A conservative sensitivity mapping both-missing pairs to failures yields baseline acceptance = 135/150 = 0.9000 and guarded = 141/150 = 0.9400; these alternate denominators are reported here only as sensitivity diagnostics, while the confirmatory inference uses the preregistered complete-pair set of 141.
sections.discussion:
Formal-estimand reconciliation and interpretation. The preregistration's natural-language H1 framed gating as a defense that would reduce attacker success (fewer unsafe configs accepted). The registered formal estimand measured paired validator acceptance (guarded − baseline). These are distinct constructs: an increase in validator acceptance may reflect successful repair of malformed drafts (reducing operator labor) rather than enabling attacker success. Our observed guarded→higher acceptance (≈4.255 percentage points) occurred because sanitizer/repair recovered reparable drafts that the baseline validator rejected. Therefore the preregistered directional attacker-success claim is not supported by the formal-estimand outcome; we report the formal estimand explicitly and caution against equating validator acceptance with attacker-centric safety without an independent semantic-safety oracle.

Operational implications and repair–gate co-design. Within the controlled synthetic setting, sanitizer + limited automated repair can recover valid, deployable configurations that unguarded generation fails to produce. Deterministic gating provides a safety boundary, but its operational effect depends critically on repair policy and validator coverage. The six discordant cases illustrate a practical trade-off: repairs enabled acceptance but could—in alternative validator encodings—accept outputs that are semantically unsafe. Consequently, practical deployment should co-design gating strictness, repair scope (which edits are permitted), and validator expressiveness to balance automation benefit against risk.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: technical failures (18/300 episodes) reduced effective sample size; paired exclusion followed preregistered rules. Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 encodes CLI grammar, required sequences and protected-interface invariants but omits some protocol-level dynamic semantics; validator acceptance is therefore a partial proxy for operational safety. External validity: single-generator (gpt-5-mini), single-validator and synthetic intents limit generalization across vendors, protocols and production traffic. Conclusion validity: the observed absolute effect is small on a high baseline (ceiling effect); detection does not automatically imply broad practical impact.

Reproducibility and protocol deviation. The archived run recorded model_configuration.json with temperature unset (temperature = null). We treat this as a protocol deviation because provider defaults could affect sampling determinism. To preserve paired comparability despite the unset temperature the pipeline used shared_initial_candidate semantics (single generation per pair) and provider-call accounting in analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json documents the actual call pattern (shared_initial_generation = 150; repair = 6). For deterministic reproduction we recommend explicitly setting sampling to deterministic values (e.g., temperature = 0) and re-executing the archived task manifest under identical provider semantics; the archived task manifest and response files permit exact replays under fixed sampling.

Recommended next steps grounded in the archived evidence. (1) Execute the preregistered benign-control to measure false-positive blocking. (2) Preregister an attacker-centric estimand coupling validator acceptance with an independent semantic-safety oracle (operational reachability checks or protocol-level dynamic simulation). (3) Diversify generators and validators across vendor CLIs and dialects. (4) Fix sampling settings (temperature) for deterministic reproductions. Each recommendation follows directly from observed artifacts and provider-call accounting.
sections.conclusion: A preregistered, artifact-backed paired experiment on a synthetic adversarial intent bank found that template-based input sanitization combined with deterministic verifier-gating and at-most-one automated repair produced a small but statistically detectable absolute increase in deterministic-validator-accepted LLM-generated configurations under the archived formal estimand (paired difference ≈ 0.04255; p = 0.03125; 95% CI [0.01418, 0.07801]). Reconciliation artifacts and per-episode validator traces indicate the six discordant pairs were associated with permitted repair calls that enabled acceptance. This formal-estimand improvement does not equal measured reduction in attacker-success under attacker-centric definitions. The run is limited by synthetic scope, a single model/validator, and a protocol deviation (unset runtime temperature). Future work should execute the benign-control, measure attacker-centric estimands with an independent semantic-safety oracle, diversify models/validators, and set explicit sampling parameters for reproducible deterministic runs. All principal numbers and reconciliation claims above are supported by archived execution and analysis artifacts referenced in Methods and Results (execution/task_manifest.jsonl; execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt; execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json; execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json; analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json; analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; analysis/condition_summary.csv; analysis/analysis_log.jsonl; execution/model_configuration.json; execution/execution_manifest.json).

limitations: Synthetic task bank and intent templates — not real production traffic or operator logs; results may not generalize to field datasets.
Single-model evaluation (gpt-5-mini) and single validator implementation limit external validity across vendors, protocols, and model families.
Validator coverage constrained to encoded safety properties (CLI grammar, required sequences, protected-interface invariants); some protocol-level or dynamic runtime semantics are not represented.
Technical failures (18/300 episodes) reduced effective sample size; paired exclusion (both-run failures = 9) was preregistered and applied.
Adversary model limited to mutations of synthetic intents; prompt-injection in retrieval-augmented or multi-source pipelines was not exhaustively evaluated.
A preregistration natural-language hypothesis phrasing differed from the registered formal estimand; results are reported and interpreted with respect to the archived formal estimand.
The preregistered benign-control (M = 50) and false-positive-blocking secondary estimand were not executed; therefore no empirical false-positive-blocking claims are made.
